title: Sequence Models: the RNN/LSTM Baseline
oneLineScope: The recurrent sequence models transformers replaced, and the two problems — vanishing gradients and inherent sequentiality — that doomed them.
prose:
To understand why the transformer exists, you need to feel what it was replacing. Through the mid-2010s the dominant framework for sequence modeling was the recurrent neural network, extended by the Long Short-Term Memory cell. These models were genuine achievements: they learned to translate, summarize, parse, and generate text well enough to drive commercial systems. Yet they had two structural problems that deepened as sequences grew longer and models grew larger, and both problems trace back to the same architectural decision — processing a sequence one step at a time.

The basic recurrent network

A plain RNN reads a sequence of tokens (a token is simply the atomic unit the model operates on — a word, subword piece, or character) one at a time, left to right. At each step t it updates a hidden state vector that is supposed to carry everything relevant from the past:

\[ h_t = f\!\left(W_x\, x_t + W_h\, h_{t-1} + b\right) \]

Here \(x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\) is the current input (typically a word embedding — a dense real-valued vector representing the token); \(h_t, h_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\) are the hidden states at steps \(t\) and \(t{-}1\), each a vector of width \(d_h\); \(W_x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_{\text{in}}}\) and \(W_h \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_h}\) are learned weight matrices shared across all steps; \(b \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\) is a bias; and \(f\) is a nonlinearity such as \(\tanh\). An output is read from \(h_t\) at each step or only at the end, depending on the task. The same weights \(W_x\) and \(W_h\) are reused at every position — that is the recurrence.

Training uses backpropagation through time (BPTT): unroll the recurrence into a computation graph with \(T\) copies of the same weights, then run ordinary backpropagation on the unrolled graph. If you know backprop, you already know BPTT — the only novelty is that the same parameter \(W_h\) appears at every step, so its gradient is the sum of contributions from all positions. This is exactly the structure you met in the backprop-era PDP literature, just applied to a sequential chain rather than a feedforward stack.

Problem 1 — vanishing and exploding gradients

The gradient of the loss with respect to a hidden state \(h_k\) far in the past flows back through the chain \(h_T \to h_{T-1} \to \cdots \to h_k\) via repeated multiplication by the Jacobian of \(f\) with respect to the previous state — at each step, roughly a factor of \(\|W_h\|\) combined with the derivative of \(f\). Across \(T - k\) steps that factor is raised to the \((T-k)\)-th power. If the dominant singular value of the relevant Jacobian is less than one, the gradient shrinks exponentially; if it exceeds one, it explodes. Bengio, Simard, and Frasconi (1994) gave the precise analysis: long-range dependencies require gradients to carry information across many steps, but the geometry of the loss surface makes this exponentially unlikely for plain nonlinear recurrences. The result is that a plain RNN reliably learns short-range patterns and unreliably learns anything that depends on context dozens of tokens away.

Exploding gradients can be patched with gradient clipping (cap the norm before the update). Vanishing gradients are the harder problem: you cannot amplify a gradient that has already decayed to nothing. This is where the LSTM intervenes.

The LSTM: a gated cell state

Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) introduced the Long Short-Term Memory cell specifically to solve the vanishing-gradient problem. The key insight is to replace the single hidden state with two objects: a cell state \(C_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\) that carries long-range information, and a hidden state \(h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\) that is the cell's filtered readout. The cell state is updated additively rather than through a squashing nonlinearity — and addition, unlike multiplication by a saturating sigmoid, does not shrink a gradient. Hochreiter called this the constant error carousel: a signal can ride the additive highway for many steps without decaying.

Three sigmoid gates, each a learned linear function of \([h_{t-1}; x_t]\) (the concatenation of the previous hidden state and the current input) followed by a logistic sigmoid \(\sigma\), control the cell:

  • The forget gate \(f_t = \sigma(W_f [h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_f) \in (0,1)^{d_h}\) element-multiplies \(C_{t-1}\), deciding what fraction of each memory dimension to keep: \(f_t \approx 0\) erases, \(f_t \approx 1\) preserves.
  • The input gate \(i_t = \sigma(W_i [h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_i)\) and a candidate update \(\tilde{C}_t = \tanh(W_c [h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_c)\) together write new content: \(i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t\) is added to the (possibly erased) cell state.
  • The output gate \(o_t = \sigma(W_o [h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_o)\) reads from the updated cell to produce the hidden state: \(h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(C_t)\).

Putting it together:

\[ C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t \] \[ h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(C_t) \]

The \(\odot\) symbol denotes element-wise multiplication. The additive structure of the \(C_t\) update is what matters for gradients: \(\partial C_t / \partial C_{t-1} = f_t\) (element-wise), which the network learns to keep near one when long-range information must be preserved, giving gradients an unattenuated path back. This is the same move as residual connections in deep feedforward networks — addition rather than repeated multiplication — but applied in the time direction.

The Gated Recurrent Unit (Cho et al., 2014) is a streamlined variant: it merges the forget and input gates into a single update gate and drops the separate cell state, yielding a two-gate cell that is cheaper to compute and often performs comparably to the LSTM on moderate sequence lengths.

Seq2seq and the fixed-vector bottleneck

With LSTMs as building blocks, Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le (2014) — and independently Cho et al. (2014) — introduced the encoder–decoder or seq2seq architecture for tasks that map one sequence to another (machine translation, summarization). An encoder LSTM reads the entire source sequence and compresses it into a single fixed-length vector — the final hidden state \(h_T \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\). A decoder LSTM is then initialized with that vector and generates the target sequence token by token, conditioning each step on the same fixed vector plus whatever the decoder has generated so far.

This works, and it was a significant step forward. But the fixed-length bottleneck is exactly what it sounds like: every word the decoder will ever need to look up — every cross-lingual correspondence, every long-distance agreement — must be packed into one vector of width \(d_h\). For short sentences this is fine. For longer ones, quality degrades measurably as the source sentence length increases. The encoder has no principled way to decide which information to prioritize, and the decoder has no way to revisit specific source positions. The next node, alignment and attention, is the direct fix: rather than compressing the source into one vector, keep all of the encoder's hidden states and let the decoder learn a soft, dynamic pointer back to whichever source positions it currently needs.

Problem 2 — inherent sequentiality

The second problem is structural and does not yield to clever gating. Because \(h_t\) depends on \(h_{t-1}\), each step of the forward pass must wait for the previous one to complete. On a sequence of length \(n\), the recurrence requires \(n\) sequential operations, regardless of how many parallel processors you have. You can parallelize across the batch and across the hidden dimension, but you cannot parallelize across time. As models grew larger and datasets grew longer through 2015–2017, this cap on throughput became the primary obstacle to scaling. GPUs are fast at matrix multiplies run in parallel; feeding them one-at-a-time recurrences wastes most of their capacity.

This is the second problem that attention solves, and it is arguably the more important one for practical training. The transformer's self-attention computes all \(n \times n\) query–key pairs simultaneously — the whole sequence in two matrix multiplies with a constant number of sequential steps. That is the property that made it possible to train on hundreds of billions of tokens within a reasonable wall-clock budget.

What comes next

The LSTM was not superseded because it failed to learn; it was superseded because what came after solved both problems at once. Attention gives every position direct access to every other position — no vanishing gradient through a chain of steps, and no sequential bottleneck. The next node (alignment and attention) traces the specific path from seq2seq's fixed-vector bottleneck to Bahdanau's soft alignment mechanism, which is the direct ancestor of the transformer's attention operation.

diagrams.caption: An RNN unrolled across time: the same weight matrices W_x and W_h apply at every step, chaining hidden states h_1 through h_T left to right. A long dashed red arrow beneath shows the gradient path back through T steps — which shrinks or explodes.
diagrams.altText: Left-to-right diagram. Input boxes x_1, x_2, x_3, ellipsis, x_T sit at the bottom. Above each, a blue hidden-state box h_1 through h_T. Blue recurrent arrows labeled W_h connect each h box to the next. Black upward arrows labeled W_x connect each x to its h. Green upward arrows lead from each h to output boxes y_1 through y_T at the top. A long red dashed arrow curves below the entire chain from h_T back to h_1 and is labeled: gradient path through T steps — shrinks or explodes.
diagrams.prompt: Structural left-to-right diagram of an RNN unrolled across time. Show four time steps explicitly: inputs x_1, x_2, x_3, then an ellipsis, then x_T, each as a labeled box at the bottom. Directly above each input box sits a hidden-state box labeled h_1, h_2, h_3, h_T. A vertical arrow labeled W_x connects each x_t up into its h_t. Horizontal arrows labeled W_h connect h_1 to h_2, h_2 to h_3, and so on through the ellipsis to h_T — these are the recurrent arrows carrying the sequential dependency. Above each h box, a vertical arrow leads to an output box y_1, y_2, y_3, y_T. On the right, add a short annotation noting that W_x and W_h are the same matrices at every step. Below the whole chain, draw a long curved dashed arrow running from h_T back to h_1, labeled: gradient path through T steps — shrinks or explodes (vanishing / exploding gradients). This bottom arrow is the visual emphasis: it shows why long-range learning is hard. Structural diagram; label every box and arrow.

diagrams.caption: Inside an LSTM cell: the cell state C_t runs as an additive highway across the top, protected by a forget gate (⊙ erase) and extended by an input gate (⊕ write). Three sigmoid gates and one tanh candidate, all fed by [h_{t-1}; x_t], control writing, retaining, and reading. The output gate produces h_t.
diagrams.altText: LSTM cell diagram. At top, a horizontal highway line from C_{t-1} on the left to C_t on the right, with two operation circles on it: a multiply circle for the forget gate and an add circle for the input gate. Below, boxes for h_{t-1} and x_t on the left feed a bus that fans out to four operations: a red sigmoid box for the forget gate f_t (arrows up to the multiply circle on the highway), a blue sigmoid box for the input gate i_t and a blue tanh box for the candidate c-tilde (their product feeds the add circle on the highway), and a green sigmoid box for the output gate o_t. On the right, a green tanh box reads from C_t, the output gate multiplies the result, and h_t emerges. A bottom note reads: cell state C_t updated additively — the constant error carousel.
diagrams.prompt: Structural diagram of a single LSTM cell. Layout: a thick horizontal line labeled C_{t-1} enters from the left and exits as C_t on the right — this is the cell-state highway at the top of the diagram. On the highway place two operation circles: first a multiply circle (⊙) where the forget gate is applied, then an add circle (⊕) where new information is written. Below the highway, on the left, two input boxes: h_{t-1} (previous hidden state) and x_t (current input). They join into a single bus [h,x] that fans out to four operations arranged left to right: (1) a sigmoid box labeled 'forget gate f_t' — its output arrow runs up to the multiply circle on the highway, annotated 'erase old memory?'; (2) a sigmoid box labeled 'input gate i_t' and a tanh box labeled 'candidate c-tilde' — their element-wise product feeds an upward arrow to the add circle on the highway, annotated 'write new info'; (3) a sigmoid box labeled 'output gate o_t' on the right. At the far right: a tanh box reads from C_t on the highway, the output gate multiplies the result (element-wise ⊙), producing h_t. Add a bottom caption note reading: 'Cell state C_t updated additively — the constant error carousel that lets gradients flow across many steps without vanishing.' Label every box, circle, and arrow. Structural diagram: precision over decoration.

bibliography.citation: Hochreiter, S., & Schmidhuber, J. (1997). Long Short-Term Memory. Neural Computation, 9(8), 1735–1780.
bibliography.annotation: The original LSTM paper. Sections 1–2 motivate the vanishing-gradient problem from first principles (the 'constant error flow' argument); §3 gives the gated cell equations. Dense but precise — skim §1–2 for the gradient analysis, §3 for the gate definitions.

bibliography.citation: Sutskever, I., Vinyals, O., & Le, Q. V. (2014). Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks. NeurIPS. arXiv:1409.3215.
bibliography.annotation: Introduces the encoder–decoder (seq2seq) architecture with LSTMs. §2 specifies the fixed-vector bottleneck; §3 gives the training details. The performance drop on long sentences (Fig. 3) is the empirical signature of the bottleneck that attention later fixes.

bibliography.citation: Bengio, Y., Simard, P., & Frasconi, P. (1994). Learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent is difficult. IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks, 5(2), 157–166.
bibliography.annotation: The foundational analysis of vanishing/exploding gradients in recurrent nets. Theorem 1 (§3) gives the formal conditions; the intuition in §2 is accessible and worth reading. This is the paper that set the problem LSTM was built to solve.

bibliography.citation: Olah, C. (2015). Understanding LSTM Networks. colah.github.io.
bibliography.annotation: The clearest visual walk-through of the LSTM cell equations, with diagram-based explanations of each gate's role and the cell-state highway. Ideal for anchoring the gate equations to intuition before reading the original paper. Does not cover seq2seq or the parallelism problem.
